issues.legal_issue: A school record does not establish a person’s date of birth merely because it contains an official entry; its source and reliability must be proved.
material_facts: The plaintiff relied on a photocopy of a school leaving certificate to establish that he was a minor when he executed a release deed.
The copy was not shown to be a certified copy of a public document.
No school official, person who recorded the date of birth, or person who supplied the information was examined; the father’s signature on the certificate was also not proved.
The plaintiff did not examine his mother or another person with special knowledge of his date of birth.
The lower courts relied on registered documents and the plaintiff’s evidence in finding that he had not proved his asserted date of birth.
issues.conclusion: The certificate did not reliably prove the plaintiff’s date of birth, and the High Court erred in treating it as sufficient proof that he was a minor when the release deed was executed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 35, 74 and 76 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, an official entry may be admissible, but admissibility does not establish its probative value. The source of the information underlying a date-of-birth entry must be proved; a certified copy is required to prove the contents of a public document by copy. Birad Mal Singhvi v. Anand Purohit held that a school entry has no evidentiary value for proving date of birth without evidence of the source of the information. Madan Mohan Singh v. Rajni Kant confirms that courts must examine the source and authenticity of official entries; Ram Suresh Singh v. Prabhat Singh states that school-register entries must be proved in accordance with law. Wali Singh v. Sohan Singh and Madhegowda v. Ankegowda did not resolve the evidentiary issue presented here.

predicates.age_disputed_in_civil_case: A party’s age at a material time is disputed in a civil case.
predicates.school_record_offered: A party offers a school record to prove the person’s date of birth.
predicates.source_of_birth_entry_not_proven: The party does not prove who supplied or recorded the date-of-birth information, or that its source had special knowledge of the date.

issues.definition: When age is disputed in a civil case and a school record is offered without proof of the source of its birth-date entry, the record does not establish the date of birth.

issues.legal_issue: A party seeking to avoid a release deed must plead the grounds on which its validity is challenged with the required particularity.
material_facts: The plaintiff’s plaint said that his signatures had been obtained on documents and that he did not know their contents.
The plaint did not specifically allege that the plaintiff was a minor when the release deed was executed, or that the deed was obtained by fraud, coercion or undue influence.
The plaintiff admitted executing the release deed and receiving consideration, and admitted leaving the family home and living with his father-in-law.
The defendants pleaded that the deed was voluntarily executed and that the plaintiff received consideration for relinquishing his rights.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff had not pleaded the grounds required to challenge the release deed, and the deed could not be treated as invalid on grounds that were not pleaded.
issues.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 requires particularised pleading of matters such as fraud, coercion and undue influence. A general assertion that signatures were obtained without knowledge of the documents does not plead those specific grounds.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_release_deed: A party in a civil suit seeks to avoid or deny the effect of a release deed.
predicates.specific_invalidity_grounds_not_pleaded: The party does not specifically plead the factual grounds on which the deed is alleged to be invalid.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to avoid a release deed in a civil suit but does not specifically plead the grounds of invalidity, the deed cannot be invalidated on those unpleaded grounds.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot reappreciate evidence in a second appeal merely to replace concurrent factual findings with another possible view.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court both found that the plaintiff had not proved his asserted date of birth and that he was not shown to have been a minor when he executed the release deed.
Both lower courts considered the school certificate and the other evidence, including registered documents and the plaintiff’s admissions.
The High Court reconsidered the certificate and reached a different factual conclusion.
The Supreme Court found that the lower courts’ findings were not based on misreading of material documents, no evidence, or a finding that no reasonable judge could reach.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact; no substantial question of law justified its reversal, and the appeal was allowed with the suit dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 confines a second appeal to substantial questions of law. Concurrent factual findings ordinarily cannot be disturbed merely because another view is possible; interference requires a recognised defect such as perversity, absence of evidence, misreading of material evidence, or inconsistency with law. The Court relied on Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Anjuman-E-Ismail Madris-Un-Niswan, Ramanuja Naidu v. V. Kanniah Naidu, Navaneethammal v. Arjuna Chetty, Secretary, Taliparamba Education Society v. Moothedath Mallisseri Illath M.N., Kondiba Dagadu Kadam v. Savitkibai Sopan Gujar, Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari and State of Rajasthan v. Shiv Dayal.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and high_court_reweighs_evidence and no_perversity_or_material_error_shown

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual finding after considering the evidence.
predicates.high_court_reweighs_evidence: The High Court reassesses the evidence to reach a different factual view.
predicates.no_perversity_or_material_error_shown: The findings are not shown to be perverse, unsupported by evidence, based on material misreading, or contrary to law.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, when the lower courts have made concurrent factual findings and the High Court reweighs the evidence without a demonstrated material defect in those findings, the High Court may not reverse them on that basis.
